In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human milk microbiome, as well as the HMO composition, is a complex system in which many factors are involved.

the composition of the bifidobacteria community of lactating mothers is influenced by the HMO composition of their milk, but the latter is not the sole factor driving the bifidobacterium community structure.

the human milk bifidobacterial microbiota, as well as its composition, is not only driven by the HMOs present in the milk, but it is also affected by the mother's health status, the infant's age, and possibly other factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HMO composition is not the only determinant of the bifidobacteria composition in breast milk, and that the presence of other milk components, as well as other factors, may play an important role.

the human milk bifidobacterial microbiota is a complex ecosystem, which is not only influenced by the milk HMO composition, but also by other milk components, the mother’s diet, as well as other factors, such as maternal age and parity.
the bifidus factor in human milk is not only a mixture of HMOs, but also a combination of bifidobacteria with different HMO degrading capabilities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HMOs are likely to represent only a minor component of the human breast-milk microbiota, and that the composition of the bifidobacteria residing in breast milk is not strictly correlated with their ability to metabolically use HMOs.

bifidobacterial communities of the human milk are highly variable, with the most abundant species differing between mothers and even between samples from the same mother, which is likely due to differences in the milk HMO composition.
the bifidogenic effect of breast milk cannot be attributed to a single species of bifidobacteria.
